Of our father among the saints, [Athanasius,] Archbishop of Alexandria, to Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis. Against those who blaspheme and say that the Holy Spirit is a creature.

1. The letter of your sacred affection was delivered to me in the desert. Although the persecution pressing upon us was bitter, and those seeking to kill us were searching hard, yet "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort" comforted us through your letter as well. For as I called to mind your affection and that of all our true friends, it seemed to me that they were there with me at that moment. For a long while I rejoiced simply holding the letter; but when I read it, I began to be disheartened again because of those who have once made it their business to fight against the truth. For you wrote, beloved and truly most dear friend, grieving yourself, that certain people who had left the Arians because of their blasphemy against the Son [?] [Variant titles from the manuscripts:] The great Athanasius's letter to Serapion, incomplete [?], concerning the Holy Spirit [?] … to Serapion the bishop, concerning the Holy Spirit … against those who say that the Holy Spirit [?] … 1. Letter to Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis, against those who blaspheme and say that he is a creature.

of God, now hold views against the Holy Spirit. They say not only that he is a creature, but also that he is one of the ministering spirits and differs from the angels only in rank. Against the Arians this is a sham fight; against the pious faith it is real opposition. For just as the Arians, by denying the Son, deny the Father also, so these people, by speaking ill of the Holy Spirit, speak ill of the Son also. The two parties have divided their resistance to the truth between them: one holds views against the Word, the other against the Spirit, and so they share the same blasphemy against the Holy Trinity. Seeing this and pondering it at length, I fell into dejection, because the devil has once again found a way to amuse himself through those who act out his madness. I had decided to keep silent at such a time. But because of your holiness's urging, and on account of their heterodoxy and satanic rashness, I have written this letter briefly, and barely managed even this much. My purpose is only that you, taking a starting point from it, may add what is lacking with the understanding you possess, and so make the refutation of this impious heresy complete.

2. Now for the Arians this notion is nothing strange. Having once denied the Word of God, they naturally utter the same slanders against his Spirit. So there is no need to say anything more to them; what has already been said against them is enough. But to those who have been deceived about the Spirit [?] … to say to them [?] … would at once cry out [?] the Spirit of God.

[?] have they tolerated [?]? For if, because of the Word's unity with the Father, they refuse to count the Son himself among the things that have come into being, and rightly hold him to be, as he truly is, the Creator of the things that were made, why do they call the Holy Spirit a creature? The Spirit has the same unity with the Son that the Son has with the Father. They have not understood this: just as by not dividing the Son from the Father they preserve the truth that God is one, so by dividing the Spirit from the Word they no longer preserve the one Godhead in the Trinity. They split it, mix into it a nature foreign and different in kind, and rank it equal with the creatures [?]. This in turn shows the Trinity to be no longer one, but composed of two different natures, because the Spirit, as they have imagined for themselves, is of a different essence. What kind of theology is this, made up of a Creator and a creature? Either it is not a Trinity but a dyad, with creation added on; or, if it is a Trinity, as indeed it is, how can they rank the Spirit of the Trinity with the creatures that come after the Trinity? That too is to divide and dissolve the Trinity. So, since they think wrongly about the Holy Spirit, they do not think rightly about the Son either. For if they thought correctly about the Word, they would also think soundly about the Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and, being proper to the Son, is given by him to the disciples and to all who believe in him. Erring in this way, they do not hold a sound faith even about the Father. For those who "resist the Spirit," as the great martyr Stephen said, deny the Son as well; and those who deny the Son do not have the Father either. 3. Where, then, you people, did you find a pretext for such daring that you are not afraid of what the Lord said: "Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness, either in this age or in the age to come"? The Arians at least misunderstood the Word's coming in the flesh and the things said on account of it, and still took from them a pretext for their own heresy; and so they were exposed as fighters against God and as truly "speaking empty words from the earth." But you, what led you astray? From whom did you hear this, and how did you fall into such error? "We read," they say, "in the prophet Amos, where God says: 'For behold, I am he who makes the thunder firm and creates spirit, and announces his Christ to men; who makes the dawn and the mist, and treads upon the high places of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name.' On that basis we were persuaded by the Arians, who say that the Holy Spirit is a creature." So you read the passage in Amos. But the saying in Proverbs, "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works," did you not read that, or did you? That one you interpret in keeping with the truth, so as not to call the Word a creature. Yet you do not interpret the passage in the prophet; simply hearing "spirit," you supposed that the Holy Spirit was being called a creature. And yet in Proverbs it is plainly Wisdom who says "He created me," and still you interpret the text, and rightly so, so as not to number the creative Wisdom among the creatures. The text in the prophet, by contrast, carries no mark referring to the Holy Spirit; it speaks simply of "spirit." The Scriptures speak of spirits in a great many different senses, and the text can have its own correct meaning. How, then, do you suppose that Amos meant the Holy Spirit? Is it out of contentiousness, or because you have been harmed by the bite of the Arian serpent, and want only to make sure you never forget to think of him as a creature?

4. Tell us, then, whether anywhere in divine Scripture you find the Holy Spirit called simply "spirit," without the addition "of God," or "of the [Apparatus:] The second Royal manuscript reads "in the present age." The same [?] the first: "Arians, although." The Canterbury manuscript [?] and the editions read "although from them," and shortly after, "and so they were exposed." Others [?] … the first [?] … [?] read as follows: "were you deceived by them? What did you hear, or what is the [?] of such error of yours? But as it is written, they say, [?]"

Father," or "my," or "of Christ himself," [?] "of the Son," or "from me," that is, from God; or with the article, so that it is not said simply "spirit" but "the Spirit"; or the very phrase "the Holy Spirit," or "Paraclete," or "of truth," that is, of the Son, who says, "I am the truth". Only then would you suppose, on hearing just "spirit," that the Holy Spirit is meant. Let us set aside for now the cases where people who have already received the Spirit are named again [?], and those who learned about the Holy Spirit beforehand and later, by way of repetition and reminder, are not unaware of whom they are hearing about even when only "the Spirit" is said, especially since even then it is said with the article. Apart from these, without the article or the addition mentioned above, the Holy Spirit would not be what is meant. Of this kind is what Paul writes to the Galatians: "This only I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?" What Spirit had they received but the Holy Spirit, who is given to those who believe and are born again "through the washing of regeneration"? And writing to the Thessalonians, "Do not quench the Spirit," he was speaking to people who knew what they had received, so that they would not through negligence quench the grace of the Spirit kindled in them. And in the Gospels, when the evangelists speak of the Saviour in human terms, on account of the flesh he took, and say, "And Jesus, full of the Spirit, returned from the Jordan," and "Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness," the meaning is the same. For Luke had said before: "Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form, like a dove." So it was clear that when "the Spirit" was mentioned, the Holy Spirit was meant. Among those in whom the Holy Spirit dwells, then, even if only "the Spirit" is said without the addition, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit is meant, especially when the article is used.

5. But you, answer the question put to you: have you found anywhere in divine Scripture the Holy Spirit

[?] called simply "spirit," without the addition mentioned above, and apart from the [?] observation we have mentioned? You will not find it so written [?]. Rather, in Genesis it is written, "And the Spirit of God was moving over the water"; and a little later, "My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh." In Numbers Moses says to the son of Nun, "Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the Lord's people were prophets, when the Lord puts his Spirit upon them!" And in Judges, concerning Othniel: "And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel." And again: "And the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah." [?] Concerning Samson it says: "The boy grew, [?] and the Spirit of the Lord began to go forth with him"; and, "The Spirit of the Lord leapt upon him." David sings: "Do not take your Holy Spirit from me." And again in the hundred and forty-second psalm: "Your good Spirit will lead me on the right path; for your name's sake, O Lord, you will give me life." In Isaiah it is written: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." Before this it was said: "Woe to you, rebellious children. Thus says the Lord: You have made plans, but not through me, and covenants, but not through my Spirit, adding sins to sins"; and again: "Hear these things: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret; when it came to pass, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." A little later he says: "And this is my covenant with them, says the Lord: my Spirit, which is upon you"; and further on he adds: "Not an elder nor an angel, but the Lord himself saved them, because he loved them and spared them; he himself redeemed them, took them up, and lifted them up all the [Apparatus:] [Scripture references, partly illegible: … Isaiah 11:10 [?] … Isaiah 59:21 [?]] One reading: "The Spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel" [?]. Ezekiel speaks thus: "And the Spirit took me up and brought me into the land of the Chaldeans, to the captivity, in a vision, by the Spirit of God." In Daniel: "God stirred up the holy Spirit of a young boy named Daniel, and he cried out with a loud voice: I am innocent of the blood of this woman." Micah says: "The house of Jacob provoked the Spirit of the Lord." Through Joel God says: "And afterwards I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh." And through Zechariah, again, it is the voice of God saying: "But receive my words and my statutes, which I command by my Spirit to my servants the prophets." And a little later, accusing the people, the prophet said: "They made their heart disobedient, so as not to listen to my law and the words which the Lord Almighty sent by his Spirit through the hands of the former prophets." These few passages we have gathered from the Old Testament.

6. Now you too should inquire into the Gospels and the writings of the apostles. You will find that there also, though "spirit" is used in a great many different senses, the Holy Spirit is named distinctively, not simply "spirit" but with the addition we spoke of. When the Lord, as I said before, was baptized in human fashion because of the flesh he bore, the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon him. Giving this Spirit to the disciples, he said, "Receive the Holy Spirit," and he taught them: "The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things." A little later he said of him: "When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me"; and again: "For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit [Apparatus:] [?] them. A little after, the same: "his holy" [?] … Felckm. 1: "And Ezekiel: And [the Spirit] took me up" [?]. Others and the editions: "And Ezekiel speaks thus." Shortly after, Gobler.: "and of the Gospels and of what," etc. Ottob.: "and about the Gospels and what." Others and the editions: "about the Gospels." … [?] shortly after: "and he taught, saying: The Holy Spirit," again. Likewise these words, "When he comes" [?], as far as [?] … The English manuscript [?] adds "and" before "the Spirit of truth."

of your Father who speaks in you"; and a little later: "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." Bringing to completion the whole of theology and our perfection, by which he joined us to himself and through himself to the Father, he commanded the disciples: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Having promised to send the Spirit to them, "he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem." And after a few days, "When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." From then on, through the laying on of the apostles' hands, the Holy Spirit was given to those who were born again. A certain Agabus prophesied by him, saying, "Thus says the Holy Spirit"; and Paul said: "…in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the Church of God, which he obtained with his own blood." And when the eunuch had been baptized, "the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away." And Peter wrote: "Obtaining the outcome of your faith, the salvation of your souls. To the Corinthians: "For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. For who knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we might know the things freely given us by God"; and a little later: "Do you not know that you are God's temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" And again: "But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God"; and again: "All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills"; and again: "Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." See also how he writes to the Galatians: "So that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith"; and again: "And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!' So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ." To the Ephesians he spoke thus: "And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption"; and again: "Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." To the Philippians he wrote with boldness: "What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice, for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my salvation, as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be put to shame in anything

"; and again: "For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus." To the Thessalonians he solemnly declares: "Therefore whoever disregards this disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you"; and to the Hebrews he writes thus: "By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first tent is still standing"; and again: "How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?" And again: "For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are defiled, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works?" And to the Thessalonians: "And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will destroy with the Spirit of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming."

7. See how the Holy Spirit is made known throughout the divine Scripture. What, then, did you see of this kind in the prophet? The "spirit" now spoken of by the prophet does not even have the article, which might at least have given you a pretext. You simply dared to invent interpretations for yourselves and to say that the spirit said to be created is the Holy Spirit himself. Yet you could have learned about the different senses of "spirit" from learned men. For "spirit" is used also of a man

Thus in Genesis: “And God brought a wind upon the earth, and the water subsided.” And in Jonah: “And the Lord raised up a wind upon the sea, and there was a great storm on the sea, and the ship was in danger of breaking apart.” In the hundred and sixth psalm it is written: “He spoke, and the stormy wind arose, and its waves were lifted high.” In the hundred and forty-eighth psalm: “Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind, which do his word.” And in Ezekiel, in the lament over Tyre: “In the heart of the sea, in many waters, your rowers brought you; the south wind has shattered you.”

8. And you too, when you read the holy Scriptures, will find that the meaning within the divine words themselves is called “spirit.” Paul writes: “who also made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” The literal text is inscribed in letters, but the meaning within it is called spirit. So too “the law is spiritual,” so that, as he said again, “we may serve not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit.” And he himself, giving thanks, said: “So then I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin.” Philip, too, wishing to turn the eunuch from the letter to the spirit, said: “Do you understand what you are reading?” Caleb is likewise attested in Numbers as having such a spirit, for God says: “But my servant Caleb, because another spirit was in him and he followed me, I will bring him into the land he entered.” Because he spoke with a mind different from theirs, he became pleasing to God. God urged the people to have such a heart through Ezekiel [?] Christ [?]. …saying: “Make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit.” Since these things are so, and so great a difference among “spirits” has been shown, you would do better, when you hear of a spirit being created, to think of one of those mentioned above, such as the one of which it is written in Isaiah: “Aram has conspired with Ephraim, and his soul was shaken, and the soul of his people, as a tree in the forest is shaken by the wind.” Such too was the wind that “the Lord raised up upon the sea” because of Jonah. For the winds also follow on thunder, as with the rain in Ahab’s time, as it is written: “And it came to pass, here and there, that the sky grew dark with clouds and wind.”

9. “But since,” they say, “the passage mentions Christ, it follows that what is called spirit must be understood as nothing other than the Holy Spirit.” Well then, you have noticed that the Holy Spirit is named together with Christ. But where did you learn to divide it from him in nature and make it alien to the Son, so that you say Christ is not a creature but say the Holy Spirit is a creature? It is absurd to name together and glorify together things that are unlike in nature. For what fellowship, or what likeness, does the creature have with the Creator? Otherwise it is time for you to number with the Son, and join to him, the creatures that came into being through him as well. It would have been enough to understand what is written as referring to the spirit of the winds, as has been said. But since you plead the mention of Christ in the passage, we must look closely at what is said, in case we find a more fitting sense for the spirit that is said to be created. What then does it mean to announce “his Christ” to men, if not that he would become man? This is the same as saying, “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” together with everything else written about his coming. And when the Word’s coming in the flesh is announced, what spirit being created should we understand, except the spirit of men that is re-created and renewed? For this is what God promised through Ezekiel, saying: “And I will give you a new heart, and [Variants:] [?] in Isaiah. [?] and editions: “such as was that which in Isaiah.” “Such too was that which,” etc. Others and editions: “Such too was” [?]. a new spirit I will give you; and I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh; and I will put my Spirit within you.” When was this fulfilled, if not when the Lord came and renewed all things by grace? See, in this passage too the difference between the spirits is shown. Our spirit is the one that is renewed; but the Holy Spirit God calls not simply “spirit” but his own, and by it ours is renewed. As the psalmist says in the hundred and third psalm: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.” If we are renewed in the Spirit of God, then the spirit now said to be created is not the Holy Spirit but ours. And if, because all things came into being through the Word, you rightly hold that the Son is not a creature, how is it not blasphemy for you to call the Spirit a creature, the Spirit in whom the Father perfects and renews all things through the Word? And if, because it is written simply that “spirit is created,” they have imagined that this is the Holy Spirit, they ought now to be persuaded that what is created is not the Holy Spirit but our own spirit, which is renewed in it. It was for this that David prayed in his psalm: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” Here it is said to be “created,” but earlier God “formed” it, as Zechariah says: “He who stretches out the heaven and lays the foundation of the earth and forms the spirit of man within him.” What he had formed earlier and what had fallen, he created anew, himself coming to be in the creature when the Word became flesh, so that, as the Apostle said, “he might create the two into one new man, created after God in righteousness and holiness of the truth.” He was not speaking of some other man made besides the one created in the image at the beginning; he was urging them to take on the mind created and renewed in Christ. This is made clear again through Ezekiel, who says: “Make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit; and why will you die, O house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the one who dies, says the Lord Adonai.”

LETTER [?] TO SERAPION [?] …that when the Paraclete was sent, his coevals, the angels, were sent with him; and then, bringing the Spirit down to the level of the angels, they rank the angels with the Trinity. For if, according to them, the angels come after the Father and the Son, plainly they belong to the Trinity [?] …the angels, and they are no longer “ministering spirits sent out for service,” nor are they sanctified; rather, they themselves sanctify others. What, then, is this great madness of theirs? Where in the Scriptures did they find the Spirit called an angel? I must repeat what I said before. The Spirit was called Paraclete, and Spirit of adoption, and Spirit of sanctification, and Spirit of God, and Spirit of Christ; but nowhere angel, nor archangel, nor spirit of service, as the angels are. Rather, together with the Son, the Spirit too is served by Gabriel, who says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Since the Scriptures do not call the Spirit an angel, what defense can they offer for such senseless audacity? Even Valentinus, who sowed this same malice among them, named the one Paraclete and the others angels, although, most foolish as he was, he too ranks the Spirit as coeval with the angels, created at the same time. “But look,” they say, “in the prophet Zechariah it is written: ‘Thus says the angel who spoke in me.’ And it is clear that he means the Spirit, the one speaking in him, is an angel.” They would not have said this if they had paid attention to what they read. For Zechariah himself, when he saw the vision of the lampstand, says: “And the angel who spoke in me answered and said: Do you not know what these are? And I said: No, Lord. And he answered and said to me: This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: Not by great power nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord Almighty.” It is evident, then, that the angel speaking to the prophet was not the Holy Spirit. He was an angel; but the Spirit is the Spirit of God Almighty. It is served by an angel, but it is inseparable from the Godhead and proper to the Word. And if they plead the apostolic text, because after… [Variants:] (93) Regii and Seguier. Editions and others [?] Zechariah [?] Regius 1 [?] “it is clear.”

[?] …Christ are mentioned “the elect angels,” let them say which of all these is the one ranked with the Trinity. They are surely not all one in number. Or which of them came down into the Jordan in the form of a dove? For those who minister are thousands upon thousands and ten thousands upon ten thousands. Or why, when the heavens were opened, is it not said, “And one of the elect angels came down,” but “the Holy Spirit”? Or why did the Lord himself, when speaking to the disciples about the end, make a distinction and say: “The Son of Man will send his angels”? And before this it had been said: “The angels ministered to him.” And again he himself says: “The angels will go out.” But when giving to the disciples he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit”; and when sending them out he said: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” He did not rank an angel with the Godhead, nor did he join us to himself and the Father in a creature, but in the Holy Spirit. And when he promised the Spirit, he did not say he would send an angel, but “the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father,” and who receives from what is his and is given.

12. Moses, for his part, knew that the angels are creatures but that the Holy Spirit is united with the Son and the Father. So when God said to him: “Go, go up from here, you and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, into the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, saying, ‘To your offspring I will give it’; and I will send my angel before you, and he will drive out the Canaanite,” he declined, saying: “If you yourself do not go with us, do not bring me up from here.” He did not want a creature to lead the people, lest they learn to worship the creation rather than God, who created all things. Indeed, having declined the angel, he begged God himself to lead them. And when God promised and said to him: “This word that you have spoken I will also do; for you have found favor before me, and I know you above all,” it is written in Isaiah: “Where is he who brought up from the land the shepherd of the sheep? [?] Bodl., Ottob.: “he did not say he would send an angel, but the”; [?] and editions, wrongly: “he did not say he would send the Spirit.” Anglicanus: “proceeds. And Moses, then, knowing.” [?] and editions: “proceeds. And knowing.”

Where is he who put the Holy Spirit in them, who led Moses by the right hand?” And a little further on he says: “The Spirit came down from the Lord and guided them. So you led your people, to make for yourself a glorious name.” Who does not see the truth from these words? When God promised to lead them, notice that he no longer promises to send an angel, but his Spirit, which is above the angels; and it is the Spirit itself that leads the people. This shows that the Spirit is not one of the creatures, nor an angel, but is above creation, united to the Godhead of the Father. For God himself, through the Word, in the Spirit, led the people. That is why throughout Scripture he says: “I brought you up out of the land of Egypt; you are witnesses whether there was a foreign god among you besides me.” And the saints say to God: “You led your people like sheep”; and, “The Lord led them in hope, and they were not afraid.” To him also they offer the hymn: “To him who led his people through the wilderness, for his mercy endures forever.” And the great Moses repeatedly says: “The Lord God who goes before you.” The Spirit of God, then, cannot be an angel or a creature, but is proper to his Godhead. For when the Spirit was among the people, God, through the Son, in the Spirit, was among them.

13. “Granted,” they say; “but why then did the Apostle, after Christ, name not the Holy Spirit but the elect angels?” One might ask them the same thing: Why did Paul name not archangels, nor cherubim, nor seraphim, nor dominions, nor thrones, nor anything else, but only elect angels? Because he did not name them, are the angels therefore archangels? Or are there only angels, and no seraphim or cherubim, no archangels, no dominions, no thrones, no principalities, nothing else? But this is to put the Apostle under compulsion over why he wrote one way and not another, and to be ignorant of the divine Scriptures, and so to wander from the truth. For look, in Isaiah it is written: “Come near to me and hear this: From the beginning I have not spoken in secret;

[?] when it came to be, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” And in Haggai: “And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, says the Lord; and let all the people of the land be strong, says the Lord; and work, for I am with you, says the Lord Almighty, and my Spirit stands in your midst.” In both prophets, mention is made only of the Lord and the Spirit. What, then, will they say about this? If, because Paul mentioned Christ and was silent about the Spirit but mentioned the elect angels, they therefore rank the Spirit among the angels, then it is time that, reading these prophetic passages, they reason even more recklessly about the one passed over in silence. For if they say that “the Lord” is the Son, what would they say about the Father? And if they say it is the Father, what would they say about the Son? May no one even entertain the blasphemy that follows from their reasoning; for they would have to say either that the one passed over does not exist, or count him among the things that were made.

14. And what would they say on hearing the Lord say: “There was a judge in a certain country who did not fear God and had no respect for man”? Since he named man after God, is this man the Son, whom the unjust judge did not respect? Or since he named man after God, is the Son third after the man, and the Holy Spirit fourth? And what if they hear the Apostle say again in the same letter: “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate, to keep the commandment spotless and blameless”? Since he is silent here about angels and the Spirit, do they doubt whether the Spirit exists, and whether angels exist? Yes, they do doubt, so far have they trained themselves in such blasphemies against the Spirit. But if they hear Scripture saying in Exodus: “He feared now,” etc. [?] Soon after [?] Regius 1 and [?].

…says the Lord. (19) Regius 1, Seguier: “about these.” [?] have: “if they say that the Lord is the Son.” Others and editions: “if they say the Lord is the Son.” [?] “to consider.” Others and editions: “according to him” and “to reckon.” “And what would those of their party say”; “There was a judge in a certain city.”

[?] the people [feared] the Lord, and believed God and his servant Moses." Will they then count Moses with God, and think not of the Son after God, but only of Moses? And what if they hear the patriarch Jacob blessing Joseph and saying, "The God who has fed me from my youth to this day, the angel who delivers me from all evils, bless these children"? Since he named an angel after God, will they conclude that the angel ranks before the Son, or that the Son is counted among the angels? Yes, they will think so again, because their hearts are corrupt. But such is not the apostolic faith, and no Christian would put up with such things. For the holy and blessed Triad is indivisible and united with itself. When the Father is mentioned, his Word is present too, and the Spirit who is in the Son. And if the Son is named, the Father is in the Son, and the Spirit is not outside the Word. For there is one grace from the Father, fulfilled through the Son in the Holy Spirit. There is one Godhead, and one God, who is over all and through all and in all. So too Paul, when he said, "I charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels," knew that the Spirit was not divided from the Son but was itself in Christ, as the Son is in the Father. He had good reason to add the elect angels. This was a solemn charge given to his disciple, and the disciple knew that what God speaks is spoken through Christ in the Spirit, while the angels serve in our affairs and watch over what each person does. So Paul wanted him to keep his teacher's instructions, knowing that those who watch over what is said were his witnesses. Or perhaps he now calls the angels to witness because of those angels who always behold the face of the Father in heaven on behalf of the little ones in the Church, so that the disciple, knowing who the guardians of the peoples are, might not neglect the Apostle's instructions.

15. Such, then, seems to me the meaning of the divine oracles, and it refutes the slander these irrational people utter against the Spirit. But, as you write, they persist in their quarrel with the truth. No longer arguing from the Scriptures, since they find nothing there, they belch from the abundance of their own hearts and say again: "If it is not a creature, nor one of the angels, but proceeds from the Father,

then it too is a son, and it and the Word are two brothers. And if it is a brother, how is the Word only-begotten? Or how are they not equal, since one is named after the Father and the other after the Son? And if it is from the Father, why is it not also said to be begotten, or said to be a son, but simply called Holy Spirit? But if the Spirit belongs to the Son, then the Father is the Spirit's grandfather." These are the games these disreputable people play. They meddle where they should not and want to search out the depths of God, which no one knows except the Spirit of God, the very Spirit they slander. We ought, then, to stop answering them. Following the apostolic command, after the admonition already given, we should avoid them as heretics. Or else we should ask them questions worthy of their own, and demand from them the kind of answer they demand from us. So let them tell us: If the Father is from a father, and another was begotten along with him, so that they are brothers from one source, what are their names? Who is their father and grandfather, and who are their ancestors? But they will say there are none. Then let them say how he is a Father, when he himself did not come from a father. Or how could he have a Son, without first being begotten as a son himself? I know the question is impious. But it is right to play the same game with those who play such games, so that the absurdity and impiety of such a question may at least make them see their own folly. For these things are not so. God forbid! It is not fitting even to ask such questions about the Godhead. For God is not like a man, that anyone should dare to ask human questions about him.

16. As I said before, we ought to keep silent on these matters and pay no attention to such people. But so that our silence does not give them an excuse for shamelessness, let them hear this. Just as one cannot speak of a father of the Father, so one cannot speak of a brother of the Son. For, as was written above, the Father did not come from some other God. And there is no other Son, for he is only-begotten. Therefore the Father, who alone is Father and is one, is Father of one only Son. Only in the Godhead do the names "Father" and "Son" stand fixed, now and always. Among human beings, someone may be called a father, yet he was born the son of another;

and someone may be called a son, yet he becomes the father of another. So among human beings the names "father" and "son" are not kept in their strict sense. Abraham, for instance, was the son of Terah and became the father of Isaac; and Isaac, the son of Abraham, became the father of Jacob. This is how human nature works. Human beings are parts of one another, and everyone who is born has a part of his father, so that he too may become father of another. But in the Godhead it is not so. For God is not like a man, and his nature cannot be divided. So he does not beget a Son by dividing himself, so that the Son might in turn become father of another, since he himself is not from a father. Nor is the Son a part of the Father. So the Son does not beget as he himself was begotten. He is the whole image and radiance of the whole. Only in the Godhead is the Father properly Father and the Son properly Son. With them, "Father" always remains Father, and "Son" always remains Son. Just as the Father could never be Son, so the Son could never become Father. And just as the Father will never cease to be the only Father, so the Son will never cease to be the only Son. It is madness, then, even to think of a brother of the Son and speak of it, or to call the Father a grandfather. For the Scriptures never called the Spirit a son, lest he be thought a brother. Nor did they call him son of the Son, lest the Father be thought a grandfather. The Son is called Son of the Father, and the Spirit is called Spirit of the Father. In this way the holy Triad has one Godhead and one faith.

17. On this count too, then, it is madness to call the Spirit a creature. If it were a creature, it would not be ranked with the Triad, for the whole Triad is one God. It is enough to know that the Spirit is not a creature and is not counted among the things that were made. Nothing alien is mixed into the Triad. It is indivisible and consistent with itself. This is enough for the faithful. This is as far as human knowledge reaches, and this is where the cherubim cover their faces with their wings. Whoever seeks beyond this and wants to probe further ignores the one who says, "Do not be over-wise, lest you be dumbfounded." What has been handed down by faith should be understood by the hearing of faith, not by human wisdom. For what

words could worthily explain things that are beyond created nature? Or what hearing could grasp what human beings may neither hear nor speak? Paul spoke this way about what he heard. And about God himself he said: "How unsearchable are his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?" Abraham did not pry or interrogate the one who spoke to him. He "believed, and it was counted to him as righteousness." So too Moses was called a faithful servant. Wisdom will not enter the scheming souls of those who hold the views of Arius, so they cannot understand or believe the truth about the indivisible and holy Triad. But that gives them no right to twist the truth as well, or to claim that whatever they cannot understand cannot exist. Their predicament is utterly absurd. Because they cannot understand how the holy Triad is indivisible, the Arians make the Son one with creation, and the Tropici in turn count the Spirit among the creatures. Since they understand nothing at all, they ought either to keep silent and stop ranking things with the creatures, the Arians the Son and the Tropici the Spirit, or else acknowledge what is written. They should join the Son to the Father and not divide the Spirit from the Son, so that the holy Triad may truly remain indivisible and of one nature. Having learned this, they ought not to presume, nor to ask in doubt how these things can be. Otherwise, if the one they ask is at a loss for an answer, they will invent wicked notions for themselves. It is impossible for any created being, and above all for us human beings, to speak worthily of the ineffable. And it is even more presumptuous, when one cannot speak, to invent new expressions for these things beyond those of the Scriptures. Besides, such an undertaking is madness, both in the one who asks and in the one who even thinks of answering. No one who asked such questions even about created things would be thought to be in his right mind.

18. Or let those who speak so readily about everything dare to answer this: How was the heaven formed, and from what matter, and how is it composed? Or how was the sun formed, and each of the stars? But why go to the things above to expose their folly, when [?]

[?] and the composition [?] is known? They could not say, since even Solomon, who had a greater share of wisdom than anyone, saw that human beings cannot find these things out. He said: "He has set the whole age in their heart, so that man cannot find out the work that God has done from beginning to end." Then, since they cannot find these things out, do they also admit that they do not exist? Yes, they will admit it, since their minds are corrupt. So one might rightly say to them: You fools, who dare anything! Why not stop prying into the holy Triad, and simply believe that it is? You have the Apostle to teach you this, when he says: "For one must first believe God, that he is, and that he rewards those who seek him." He did not say how he is, but only that he is. If even this does not shame them, let them say how the Father is, and then they may learn how his Word is too. "But it is absurd," they will say, "to ask such questions about the Father." Then let them hear that it is just as absurd to ask such questions about his Word.

19. Since such an undertaking is pointless and, more than that, madness, let no one ask such things any longer. Let him only learn what is in the Scriptures, for the illustrations they set out on this subject are sufficient and adequate. The Father, then, is called fountain and light. "They have forsaken me," it says, "the fountain of living water." And again in Baruch: "Why is it, Israel, that you are in the land of your enemies? You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom." And in John: "Our God is light." The Son, in relation to the fountain, is called river: "The river of God is full of water." In relation to the light, he is called radiance, as Paul says: "He is the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his being." The Father, then, is light and the Son is his radiance. We should not hesitate to say the same things about them often. So we may see the Spirit too in the Son, the Spirit in whom we are enlightened. "That he may give you," it says, "the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart being enlightened." And when we are enlightened by the Spirit, it is Christ who enlightens us in him. "That was the true light," it says, "which enlightens every man coming into the world." Again, since the Father is fountain and the Son is called river, we are said to drink the Spirit. For it is written

that "We were all made to drink of one Spirit." And when we drink the Spirit, we drink Christ. "For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." Again, since Christ is the true Son, we become sons when we receive the Spirit. "For you did not receive," it says, "a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption." And since we are made sons by the Spirit, it is clear that it is in Christ that we are called children of God. "For as many as received him, to them he gave power to become children of God." Then, since the Father, as Paul said, is the only wise one, the Son is his wisdom. "For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God." And since the Son is wisdom, when we receive the Spirit of wisdom we have the Son, and in him we become wise. So it is written in the hundred and forty-fifth psalm: "The Lord sets the prisoners free; the Lord makes the blind wise." And when the Spirit is given to us ("Receive the Holy Spirit," said the Savior), God is in us. John wrote: "If we love one another, God abides in us. By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit." And since God is in us, the Son is in us too. The Son himself says: "I and the Father will come and make our home with him." Further, since the Son is life ("I am the life," he says), we are said to be given life in the Spirit. "For he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead," it says, "will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you." And when we are given life in the Spirit, Christ himself is said to live in us. "I have been crucified with Christ," it says. "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." And again, the Son said that the works he did were the Father's doing: "The Father who abides in me does the works. Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father in me, or else believe me because of the works themselves." In the same way, Paul said that what he did in the power of the Spirit were Christ's works: "For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders [?]

[?] from the Father, or the Spirit from the Son or from the Father himself? Or who is so presumptuous as to say that the Triad is unlike itself and made of different natures, or that the Son is of an essence alien to the Father, or that the Spirit is foreign to the Son? But someone might ask again, inquiring how these things can be. How, when the Spirit is in us, is the Son said to be in us? And when the Son is in us, how is the Father said to be in us? Or how, when there is a whole Triad, is the Triad signified in one? Or how, when one is in us, is the Triad said to be in us? Let him first separate the radiance from the light, or wisdom from the wise one, or else tell us how these things are. If he cannot do this, it is far greater madness and presumption to ask such things about God. For, as has been said, the Godhead is not handed down through proofs in words. It is handed down in faith, and in reverent and devout reasoning. Paul preached even the things concerning the saving cross "not in wisdom of words, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power." And "in paradise" he "heard inexpressible words, which it is not lawful for a man to speak." Who, then, can speak out about the holy Triad itself? Still, such perplexity can be remedied, first and foremost by faith, and then also by the illustrations mentioned above: image and radiance, fountain and river, being and exact imprint. For just as the Son is in the Spirit as in his own image, so also the Father is in the Son. Divine Scripture, consoling us for our inability to explain such things in words or to grasp them, has given us these illustrations. Because of the unbelief of the presumptuous, they let us speak more simply and without danger, and think with allowance made for our weakness. They let us believe that there is one sanctification, which comes from the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit. For just as the Son is only-begotten, so also the Spirit, given and sent from

the Son, is itself one and not many, nor one made out of many, but the Spirit alone. Since the Son, the living Word, is one, his sanctifying and enlightening living activity and gift must also be one, perfect and complete. This gift is said to proceed from the Father, because it shines forth from the Word, who is confessed to be from the Father, and is sent and given by him. Indeed, the Son is sent by the Father. "For God so loved the world," it says, "that he sent his only-begotten Son." And the Son sends the Spirit. "If I go away," he says, "I will send the Paraclete." The Son glorifies the Father, saying, "Father, I have glorified you." And the Spirit glorifies the Son. "He will glorify me," he says. The Son says, "What I heard from the Father, these things I speak to the world." And the Spirit receives from the Son. "For he will take what is mine and declare it to you," he says. The Son came in the name of the Father. "But the Holy Spirit," says the Son, "whom the Father will send in [my] name [?]

21. The Spirit stands in the same order and has the same nature in relation to the Son as the Son has in relation to the Father. So how can anyone who calls the Spirit a creature avoid thinking the same about the Son? If the Spirit is a creature of the Son, it would follow for them to say that the Word of the Father is also a creature. It was by imagining such things that the Arians fell into the Judaism of Caiaphas. But if those who say such things about the Spirit claim not to hold Arius's views, let them shun his words too, and stop committing impiety against the Spirit. The Son is in the Father, and the Father is in him. He is not a creature but belongs properly to the Father's essence, as you yourselves claim to say. In the same way, the Spirit is in the Son, and the Son is in the Spirit. It is not right to rank the Spirit with the creatures, or to divide him from the Word and so make the Triad incomplete. As for the sayings of the prophet and the Apostle, whose meaning they distorted and so deceived themselves, it is enough to use these points to refute the [?] that comes from the ignorance of the Tropici

…one. Now let us look at what the divine Scriptures say about the Holy Spirit taken on its own. Like skilled money-changers, let us test whether the Spirit has anything in common with creatures, or whether he belongs to God. Then we can call him either a creature, or something other than the creatures, belonging to the Godhead in the Trinity and one with it. Perhaps this will put them to shame, once they learn how far the blasphemous phrases they have invented clash with the divine oracles.

22. Creatures, then, have come into being out of nothing, and their coming-to-be had a beginning. For “in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” and all that is in them. But the Holy Spirit is said to be from God. “For no one,” he says, “knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him. In the same way no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God.” From what has been said, then, what kinship does the Spirit have with creatures? Creatures once did not exist. But God is He who is, and the Spirit is from him. What is from God cannot be from what is not, nor can it be a creature. Otherwise, by their reasoning, the One from whom the Spirit comes would also be thought a creature. Who will put up with fools like these, who also say in their heart that there is no God? For if no one knows the things of a man except the spirit in him, and in the same way no one knows the things of God except the Spirit in him, then surely it is blasphemous to call a creature the Spirit who is in God and searches even the depths of God. From this such a person will learn to say that the spirit of a man is outside the man himself, and that the Word who is in the Father is a creature. Again, the Spirit is the Spirit of holiness and renewal, and is called so. For Paul writes: “declared Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.” And again he says: “But you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.” And when writing to Titus
[?] …let us test. In the unbegotten (Regius 2: unoriginate) Trinity of the Godhead [?]. But God is He who is, having brought all things into being out of nothing [?] … I say … [?]

he said: “But when the kindness and love [?]…”

23. That which is not sanctified by another and does not share in sanctification, but is itself shared in, and in which all creatures are sanctified: how could it be one of all things, belonging to those who share in it? Anyone who says this must also say that the Son, through whom all things came into being, is one of all things. He is called the life-giving Spirit. “For he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead,” he says, “will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.” The Lord is life itself and “the author of life,” as Peter said. And the Lord himself said: “The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life. Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.” But creatures, as has been said, are given life through him. That which does not share in life, but is itself shared in and gives life to creatures: what kinship does it have with things that have come into being? How could it be one of the creatures at all, when it is in him that they are given life by the Word? The Spirit is called an anointing, and he is a seal. For John writes: “The anointing you received from him remains in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you. But as his anointing” (that is, his Spirit) “teaches you about all things.” In the prophet Isaiah it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me.” And Paul says: “In him you also, having believed, were sealed for the day of redemption.” But creatures are sealed and anointed by him, and [?] … (first manuscript): “from works which were in righteousness,” etc. [?] (another): “from works which were in righteousness,” etc. The Anglican manuscript: “from works which were of righteousness,” etc. But the editions and the other manuscripts: “from works of righteousness which we have done”

[?] …are taught all things. If the Spirit is the anointing and the seal with which the Word anoints and seals all things, what likeness or affinity do the anointing and the seal have with what is anointed and sealed? In this respect too, then, he cannot be one of all things. The seal is not one of the things sealed, nor is the anointing one of the things anointed. It belongs to the Word who anoints and seals. The anointing carries the fragrance and breath of the one who anoints, and those who are anointed share in it and say: “We are the fragrance of Christ.” The seal bears the form of Christ who seals, and those who are sealed share in it and are formed according to it. As the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” Sealed in this way, we rightly become partakers of the divine nature too, as Peter said. And so all creation partakes of the Word in the

24. And through the Spirit we are all said to be partakers of God. “Do you not know,” he says, “that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are.” If the Holy Spirit were a creature, we could have no participation in God through him. We would instead be joined to a creature and become strangers to the divine nature, sharing in it in no way. [?] partakers of Christ and partakers of God, this shows that the anointing and the seal in us are not of the nature of things that have come into being. They belong to the Son, who joins us to the Father through the Spirit who is in him. John taught this, as was said above, when he wrote: “By this we know that we remain in God and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” If by participation in the Spirit we become partakers of the divine nature, anyone would be mad to say that the Spirit is of created nature and not

of the nature of God. This is why those in whom he comes to dwell are deified. And if he deifies, there can be no doubt that his nature is of God. Still more clearly, to refute this heresy, the hundred and third psalm sings, as we said before: “You will take away their spirit, and they will die and return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.” And Paul writes to Titus: “Through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ.” If the Father creates and renews all things through the Word in the Holy Spirit, what likeness or kinship does the Creator have with creatures? How could that in which all things are created be a creature at all? Such slander brings blasphemy against the Son in its train. Those who call the Spirit a creature must say that the Word too, through whom all things are created, is a creature. The Spirit is called the image of the Son, and he is that image: “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” Since even they admit that the Son is not a creature, his image cannot be a creature either. Whatever the image is, the one whose image it is must be the same. That is why the Word is rightly and fittingly confessed not to be a creature: he is the image of the Father. So whoever counts the Spirit among the creatures will surely count the Son among them too, and in this he also blasphemes the Father, by blaspheming his image.

25. The Spirit, then, is other than the creatures, and he has been shown rather to belong to the Son and not to be foreign to God. As for that clever question of theirs, “If the Spirit is from God, why is he not also called a Son?”, it has already been shown above to be rash and reckless, and it is shown to be so now no less. Even if Scripture did not call him Son, but Spirit of God, he is said to be in God himself and from God himself, as the Apostle wrote. This is how the Fathers understood it when they confessed at the Council of Nicaea that the Son is consubstantial with the Father and from the Father's substance. They rightly perceived that a created substance could never say: "All that the Father has is mine." For since it has a beginning of its coming into being, it does not possess "is" and "was" eternally. Therefore, since the Son has these things, and all the things of the Father mentioned above are the Son's, the Son's substance cannot be created; it must be consubstantial with the Father. Besides, a created substance could not, on this account, be capable of receiving what is proper to God. And what is proper to him are the things by which God is known, such as being Almighty, being "He Who Is," being unchangeable, and the others mentioned above. Otherwise God himself would appear, as the senseless would have it, to be consubstantial with creatures, having what creatures too can have. 6. As the Lord himself said, “The Paraclete will not speak on his own; he will speak whatever he hears, for he will take from what is mine and declare it to you.” He breathed on the disciples and gave them the Spirit from himself, and in this way the Father poured it out on all flesh, as it is written. We shall find that the Spirit has the same proper relation to the Son that we have known the Son to have to the Father. The Son says, “All that the Father has is mine.” In the same way we shall find that all these things are also in the Spirit, through the Son. And as the grace of the Trinity is one, so the Trinity is indivisible. One can see this in the case of holy Mary herself. The angel Gabriel was sent to announce the coming descent of the Word upon her, and he said, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.” He knew that the Spirit was in the Word, and so he immediately added, “and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. In the same way, when the Spirit comes to be in us, the Son and the Father will come and make their dwelling in us. For the Trinity is indivisible and its Godhead is one, and there is one God, over all and through all and in all. This is the faith of the catholic Church. The Lord founded and rooted it in the Trinity when he said to the disciples, “Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” If the Spirit were a creature, he would not have ranked it with the Father, so that…

…the Triad would be unlike itself, with something foreign and alien ranked alongside it. For what was God lacking, that he should take on something of an alien essence and be glorified together with it? God forbid! It is not so. "I am full," he himself said. That is why the Lord himself ranked the Spirit with the name of the Father: to show that the Holy Triad is not made up of different things, that is, of Creator and creature, but that its Godhead is one. Having learned this, Paul taught that the grace given in it is one, saying: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." And just as there is one baptism, so too there is one faith. For whoever believes in the Father knows the Son in the Father, and the Spirit not outside the Son; and for this reason he believes also in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, since the Godhead of the Triad is one, known from the one Father. 7. This, then, is the stamp of the catholic faith. As for those who blaspheme the Spirit and call him a creature, if they do not change their minds because of what has been said, let them at least sink down in shame at what is about to be said. If there is a Triad, and the faith is in a Triad, let them say whether it is always a Triad, or whether there was a time when there was no Triad. If, then, the Triad is eternal, the Spirit is not a creature, since he exists eternally with the Word and is in him. For of creatures there was a time when they were not. But if he is a creature, and creatures come from nothing, it is clear that there was a time when there was no Triad, but a Dyad. And what could anyone say more impious than this? They are saying that the Triad came about through change and progress: that it was a Dyad, and waited for a creature to come into being, so that it might be ranked with the Father and the Son and the Triad might come about. God forbid that such a thing should ever even enter the minds of Christians! For just as the Son, being eternal, is not a creature, so, since the Triad is eternal, there is no creature in it; therefore the Spirit is not a creature. For as it always was, so it is now; and as it is now, so it always was, and is: the Triad, and in it the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And there is one God, the Father, who is over all, and through all, and in all, who is blessed for ever. Amen. So, as you asked, I have written these things down briefly and sent them to you. I have also read the letter your Reverence has just written, and, greatly astonished at the shamelessness of the heretics, I saw that nothing fits them so well as the Apostle's injunction: "After a first and a second admonition, have nothing more to do with a heretical man, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned." What was said before, then, should have been enough; having received so many proofs, they should have been content to stop their blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. But they were not content; they are shameless once again, to show that, having practised fighting over words and now fighting against the Spirit, they will shortly be dead from their own irrationality. For just as the Saviour, when they questioned him maliciously, asked them a question in return so that they might perceive their own ill will, so, since these people too ask such things, let them tell us themselves—or rather, let them answer when they are questioned in the same way that they question. For since, when they speak, they perhaps do not understand their own inventions, perhaps on hearing them they may recognize their own folly. If the Holy Spirit is not a creature, as has been shown above, but is in God and is given from God, then he too is a son, and the two are brothers, he and the Son; and if the Spirit is of the Son, and the Spirit receives all things from the Son, as he himself has said, and the Son "breathed on" the disciples and gave him to them (for you too confess these things), then the Father is a grandfather and the Spirit is his grandson. For the prophets prophesied whenever the Word of God came to them. And besides this, since all things came into being through the Word, and without him not one thing came into being, and "God founded the earth by wisdom," and "made all things in wisdom" (and it is written, as has been shown above, "You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created"), then either the Spirit is the Word, or God made all things in two, in Wisdom and in the Spirit. What do you say to this, you who say everything so glibly? What are you reasoning among yourselves? Or, seeing yourselves at a loss, do you find fault with such questions? Then first condemn yourselves (for you are the ones accustomed to ask such things), and obey the Scriptures; and since you are at a loss for an answer, learn at last: in the Scriptures the Spirit is not named Son, but Holy Spirit and Spirit of God. And just as the Spirit is not named Son, so neither is it written of the Son that he is the Holy Spirit. For the Son is the proper offspring of the essence and nature of the Father, and this is what that name signifies. And the Spirit, being called "of God" and being in him, is not foreign to the nature of the Son, nor to the Godhead of the Father. This is why in the Triad—in the Father, in the Son, and in the Spirit himself—there is one Godhead, and in this same Triad there is one baptism and one faith. Indeed, when the Father sends the Spirit, the Son breathes on the disciples and gives him to them, since all that the Father has belongs to the Son. If anyone asks this, such a person would be mad, searching into what is unsearchable and ignoring the Apostle, who says: "For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?" Besides, what God has named, who will dare to rename? Otherwise let him take up the things of creation. Let them say, since creation came about by the same nod, why one thing is the sun and others the heaven and the earth and the sea and the air. But if this is impossible even for fools (for each thing remains as it was made), much more do the things above creation have an eternal permanence, and it is not otherwise than that the Father is Father and not grandfather, and the Son is Son of God and not father of the Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit, and not grandson of the Father, nor brother of the Son. These things being shown thus, anyone would be mad to ask, "Is the Spirit, then, also a Son?" Nor, because it is not written so, should anyone for that reason remove him from the nature and property of God; but let him believe as it is written, and not say, "Why like this and not like that?"—lest, reasoning in this way, he begin to ponder and say, "Where, then, is God, and how does he exist?" and then hear: "The fool has said in his heart, There is no God." For what is handed down by faith is to be known without curious prying. The disciples, at any rate, when they heard, "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," [?] … the Spirit third, or why a Triad at all; but as they heard, so they believed; and they did not ask, as you do, "Is the Spirit, then, a Son?" Nor, when the Lord named the Spirit after the Son, did they ask, "Is the Father, then, a grandfather?" For they did not hear "into the name of the grandfather," but "into the name of the Father," and they preached this faith everywhere, reasoning rightly. For it was not possible to speak otherwise than as the Saviour spoke: of himself as Son, and of the Spirit as Holy Spirit; nor is it lawful to interchange them from the order in which they have been ranked, just as with the Father. For as it is not permitted to speak of him otherwise than as Father, so it is impious to ask whether the Spirit is a Son, or the Son the Spirit. For this reason Sabellius was judged alien to the Church, for daring to apply the name "Son" to the Father, and to the Son the name of "Fa[ther]"… (Notes: Rom. 11:34; Ps. 14:1. [Variant:] "sea, air." Shortly after, Reg. and Seguer.: "to fools.")

…Eunomians, and Eudoxians, and Eusebians. For once they have taken up the part of the Arian heresy, they will never restrain their tongue from impiety. For who handed these things down to them? Who taught them? No one from the divine Scriptures; rather, such derangement has come out of the abundance of their heart. 6. For if, since the Spirit is not a creature (for this has been shown), you ask, "Is the Spirit, then, a Son?", it is time for you, having learned that the Son is not a creature (for through him the things that come into being were created), to ask, "Is the Son, then, a Father?" Or else this: "Is the Son, then, the Spirit, and is the Son himself the Holy Spirit?" Those who reason in this way will be outside the Holy Triad and will be judged godless, changing the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and transferring it as they please after the likeness of human generation, talking of grandsons and grandfathers, and fashioning for themselves the theogony of the Greeks. But this is not the faith of the Church; rather, as the Saviour said, it is into Father and Son and Holy Spirit: a Father who cannot be called grandfather, a Son who cannot be called father, and a Holy Spirit named in no other way than this. In this faith there is no interchanging of names; but the Father is always Father, and the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always is, and is called, Holy Spirit. With human beings it is not so, even if the Arians imagine such things. For as it is written, "God is not as a man," so one might say that men are not as God. For among men the father is not always father, nor the son always son. The same man becomes father of a son, yet was himself born son of another; and the son, being son of a father, becomes father of another. Abraham, for example, being son of Nahor, became father of Isaac; and Isaac, being son of Abraham, became father of Jacob. For each, being part of his parent, is born a son, and himself becomes father of another. But in the Godhead it is not so, since God is not as a man. The Father, then, is not from a father; therefore he does not beget one who will become father of another. Nor is the Son part of the Father; therefore he is not begotten in order to beget a son. Hence in the Godhead alone the Father, being properly and alone Father, is and was and always is [?]; and the Son is properly and alone Son. And in their case it holds firm that the Father always is, and is called, Father, and the Son always Son; and the Holy Spirit too is always Holy Spirit; and we believe that he is of God and is given from the Father through the Son. (Note 60: The same [manuscripts read] "concerning Eunomius, Eudoxius and Eusebius.")

For in this way the Holy Triad remains unchanging, known in one Godhead. So whoever asks, "Is the Spirit, then, a Son?", imagines that the name can be changed, and brings madness upon himself. And whoever asks, "Is the Father, then, a grandfather?", inventing a name for the Father, goes astray in his heart. To answer the shamelessness of the heretics any further is not safe, for that would be to fight against the apostolic exhortation; it is better rather to admonish them, as he himself enjoined. 7. This is enough to refute your foolish talk. Stop making a game of the Godhead. For it is characteristic of those who play games to ask about what is not written and to say, "Then the Spirit is a Son, and the Father a grandfather." This is how the one in Caesarea and the one in Scythopolis joke. It is enough for you to believe that the Spirit is not a creature, but is the Spirit of God, and that in God there is a Triad: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. And one must not apply the name Father to the Son, nor is it permitted to say that the Spirit is the Son, or that the Son is the Holy Spirit; but it is as has been said, and there is one Godhead in this Triad, and one faith, and one baptism given in it, and one perfection, in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom be glory and power to the Father with the Holy Spirit, to all the ages of ages.

…[you will not] find fault with me, knowing both my eagerness and my weakness. The saying, then, is this. When so many signs were taking place in the Gospel, the Pharisees said: "This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons." [?] … who have received a share of him in the gift of baptism. So when catechumens and pagans sin, they sin against the Son, since he is in them, as has been said. Even so, they can receive forgiveness when they are counted worthy of the gift of regeneration. But when the baptized sin, he says that such lawlessness reaches to the Holy Spirit, because the one who sinned had already come to be in him. For this reason the punishment against such a person cannot be pardoned.
11. Theognostus also adds the following: "One who has crossed the first boundary and the second might be judged to deserve a lesser punishment. But one who has also disregarded the third could no longer obtain pardon." By the first and second boundaries he means the instruction about the Father and the Son. By the third he means the Word handed down at the perfecting, when one comes to share in the Spirit. To confirm this, he cites what the Saviour said to the disciples: "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot yet bear them. But when the Holy Spirit comes, he will teach you." Then he says: "The Saviour speaks with those who cannot yet take in perfect things, coming down to their littleness, while the Holy Spirit is present with those who are being perfected. Surely no one would conclude from this that the Spirit's teaching surpasses the Son's instruction. The point is that the Son comes down to the imperfect, while the Spirit is the seal of those being perfected. In the same way, blasphemy against the Spirit is inescapable and unpardonable not because the Spirit is superior to the Son. It is because the imperfect can be pardoned, while those who have tasted the heavenly gift and been perfected have no plea or excuse for pardon left." That is what these men say.
12. But from what I have learned, I think the meaning of each of them needs some careful testing and examination. Perhaps a deeper sense lies hidden in the very things they have said. For it is clear that the Son, being in the Father, is in those in whom the Father is, and the Spirit is not absent either. The holy, blessed and perfect Trinity is indivisible. Moreover, if all things came into being through the Son, and all things hold together in him, how could he be outside the things made through him? And since they are not far from him, it follows that he too is in all of them. So of necessity anyone who sins and blasphemes against the Son also sins against the Father

and against the Holy Spirit. As for the holy washing, if it were given into the Holy Spirit alone, it might reasonably be said that the baptized sin against the Spirit alone. But it is given into the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and that is how each of the baptized is perfected. So again it necessarily follows that those who transgress after baptism direct their blasphemy against the holy and indivisible Trinity. It is also right to consider the following. If the Lord had been speaking to people who had received the washing of regeneration (I mean the Pharisees) and who already shared in the gift of the Holy Spirit, such an interpretation would be somewhat plausible: they could be thought of as having relapsed and offended against the Holy Spirit. But they had not received the washing. They had even despised the baptism of John. How then could he blame them [?] for blaspheming against the Holy Spirit, in whom they had not yet come to share? Nor was the Lord simply teaching when he said these things, or threatening punishment against people in the future. He was truly accusing the Pharisees then and there, as already guilty of so great a blasphemy, when he spoke this saying. Since the Pharisees were accused in this way before they had received baptism, the saying cannot refer to those who transgress after the washing. This is especially so because he accused them not simply of sins but of blasphemy. And there is a difference: whoever sins breaks the law, but whoever blasphemes commits impiety against the Godhead itself. The Saviour had earlier accused them of many offences. They broke God's commandment about parents for the sake of money, they set aside the words of the prophets, and they made the house of God a house of trade. Yet even so he urged them to repent. But when they said, "He casts out demons by Beelzebul," he no longer called this simply a sin. He called it a blasphemy so great that the punishment for those who dare such things is inescapable and unpardonable.
13. Besides, suppose this saying was spoken about those who sin after the washing, and for them the penalty for their offences cannot be pardoned. How then does the Apostle confirm his love for the man in Corinth who repented, and why is he in labour again for the Galatians who had relapsed, until Christ is formed in them again? By saying "again" he also shows that they had earlier been perfected in the Spirit. And why do we blame Novatus for abolishing repentance and Spirit the Holy. Felckmann: [?] and also into the Father.
