for claiming that those who sin after the washing have no pardon, if the saying was spoken about those who sin after the washing? For what is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews does not shut sinners out of repentance. It shows that the baptism of the catholic Church is one, and there is no second. He was writing to Hebrews. Following the custom of the law, they might have thought that there are many baptisms, even daily ones, on the grounds of repentance. So he urges them to repent, but declares that there is one renewal through baptism and no second, as he also says in another letter: "One faith, one baptism." He did not say that it is impossible to repent. He said it is impossible for us to be renewed on the grounds of repentance. And there is a great difference between the two. Whoever repents stops sinning but still bears the scars of his wounds. Whoever is baptized puts off the old self and is renewed, born from above by the grace of the Spirit.

Perhaps from it I may be able to grasp the sense of the passage. he rebuked the Jews: "Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from the Father?" These things did not happen separately according to the character of what was done, as though the things of the body were shown apart from the Godhead and the things of the Godhead apart from the body. Everything happened together, and it was one Lord who did these things, wondrously, by his own grace. He spat as a man, but the spittle was divine, for with it he made the man blind from birth see. And wishing to show that he was God, he signified this with a human tongue, saying, "I and the Father are one"; and he healed merely by willing it. Yet he stretched out a human hand to raise Peter's mother-in-law when she had a fever, and to raise the synagogue ruler's daughter, who had already died, from the dead

15. Heretics, then, have raved in keeping with their own lack of learning. Some looked at the Saviour's bodily aspects and denied "In the beginning was the Word." Others contemplated what belongs to the Godhead and ignored "The Word became flesh." But the faithful and apostolic person knows the Lord's love for humankind. When he sees the signs of the Godhead, he marvels at the Lord in the body. And when he observes the properties of the body, he is struck with even greater amazement, perceiving the working of the Godhead in them. This is the Church's faith. So when some look at the human things and see the Lord thirsting, toiling or suffering, and simply babble against the Saviour as if he were a man, they sin greatly. Yet if they quickly repent they can still receive pardon, since they have the weakness of the body as their excuse. (They even have the Apostle granting them pardon and, as it were, stretching out a hand to them when he says, "And undeniably great is the mystery of godliness: God was revealed in the flesh.") Again, when some contemplate the works of the Godhead and doubt the nature of his body, they too sin most grievously. Although they see him eating and suffering, they imagine he was a phantom. The Saviour was displaying the works of the Father: he raised the dead, gave sight to the blind, made the lame walk, opened the ears of the deaf, made the mute speak, and showed that creation was subject to him by commanding the winds and walking on the sea itself. The crowds were amazed and glorified God, but the admirable Pharisees said that such works belonged to Beelzebul. The fools were not ashamed to transfer the power of God to the devil. So the Saviour, consistently, declared that their blasphemy was unpardonable and inescapable. As long as they looked at the human things and stumbled in their understanding, he bore with them. They said, "Is this not the carpenter's son?" and "How does this man know letters, when he has never studied?" and "What sign do you do about yourself?" and "Let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him." Since they were sinning as against a Son of Man, he grieved at the hardness of their hearts and said, "If you too had known the things that make for peace." Indeed, when the doorkeeper spoke to the great Peter about him as a man, and Peter answered as he did, the Lord pardoned him when he wept. But they fell and fell further, raving even more, until they said that the works of God belonged to Beelzebul. Then he no longer bore with them, for they were blaspheming against his Spirit by saying that the one who did these things was not God but Beelzebul. while looking at the order of the world and the providence over it, that creation too was made by Beelzebul, that the sun rises in obedience to the devil, and that the stars circle in heaven because of him. For just as these things are God's works, so those deeds too were the works of the Father. If those were Beelzebul's, then these are necessarily Beelzebul's as well. And where would that leave "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth"? But there is nothing strange about such madness on their part. The fathers who shared this opinion did the same in the wilderness, shortly after they came out of Egypt. They fashioned a calf, credited it with the benefits God had given them, and said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." Because of this blasphemy, many of those who dared such things were killed at the very outset, and not just a few. And God declared, "On whatever day I visit, I will bring their sin upon them." As long as they merely grumbled about bread and water, he bore with them, as a nurse carries her own son. But when they raved further, and, as the Spirit sings against them, "They exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass," then at last they had dared what cannot be pardoned, and they were struck down. As Scripture says, this was because of the calf that Aaron made.
17. The Pharisees now dared similar things, and they received from the Savior the same sentence that the Beelzebul they imagined has already received and still holds: they are to be consumed eternally along with him in the fire prepared for him. He did not say these things to compare blasphemy against himself with blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, as if the Spirit were greater and blasphemy against the Spirit therefore carried greater guilt. God forbid! He had already taught that everything the Father has belongs to the Son, and that the Spirit will receive from the Son and will glorify the Son. It is not the Spirit who gives the Son. The Son supplies the Spirit to the disciples, and through them to those who believe in him. So that is not what the Saviour meant. The Lord spoke these words as of blasphemy directed against himself in both respects, the one

lesser and the other far greater. For the Pharisees themselves said both. Seeing him as a man, they reviled him: "Where did this man get this wisdom?" and "You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?" And when they saw the works of the Father, they not only denied his Godhead but said in its place that Beelzebul was in him and that the works were Beelzebul's. Both things were said against him: the lesser blasphemy against his humanity and the greater against his Godhead. That is why he declared that for the greater one their punishment could not be escaped. Indeed, when he encouraged the disciples by saying, "If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul," he was saying that he himself was the master of the house, the one whom even the Jews were blaspheming in this way.

But the works the Lord did were no longer for human beings to do; they were for God. 19. Looking closely at the passage itself also seems to me to point in this direction. It shows that both blasphemies reach him, and that he was speaking about himself when he said both "Son of Man" and "Spirit." By "Son of Man" he showed his bodily nature, and by "Spirit" he revealed his spiritual, intelligible and most true Godhead. He linked the sin that can be pardoned with the Son of Man to point to his bodily nature. He declared that the unpardonable blasphemy reaches the Spirit, contrasting the Spirit with the bodily, in order to show his own Godhead. I have seen the same pattern in the Gospel according to John as well. When the Lord was speaking about eating his body, and saw that many were offended by it, he said: "Does this offend you? What then if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh is of no use at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life." Here too he spoke of both in himself, flesh and spirit. He distinguished the spirit from what belongs to the flesh, so that they would believe not only in what could be seen of him but also in what could not be seen, and would learn that what he says is not fleshly but spiritual. For how many people would his body have been enough to feed, that it should become food for the whole world? That is why he mentioned the Son of Man's ascent into

heaven: to draw them away from a bodily understanding, so that they would then learn that the flesh he spoke of is heavenly food from above, spiritual nourishment given by him. "For the words that I have spoken to you," he says, "are spirit and life." This is as if he said: "What is shown and given for the salvation of the world is the flesh that I wear. But this flesh and its blood will be given to you by me spiritually as food, so that it may be distributed spiritually within each of you and become a safeguard for all, leading to the resurrection of eternal life." In the same way the Lord drew the Samaritan woman away from things of the senses by saying that God is Spirit, so that she would no longer think of God in bodily terms but spiritually. In the same way also the prophet, seeing the Word who became flesh, said, "The Spirit of our face is Christ the Lord." He said this so that no one would judge from what can be seen that the Lord is a mere man. Hearing "Spirit" as well, they would know that the one who is in the body is God.

…seeing his works being done by the Holy Spirit, and saying that the one who does such things is not God and the Son of God, but ascribing them to Beelzebul, he openly blasphemes, denying his Godhead. For in the Gospel saying too, as has often been said, when he says "Son of Man" he points to what in him is according to the flesh and human, so that when he says "the Spirit" he may show that the Holy Spirit, in whom he worked all things, is his own. That is why, while doing the works, he said: "If you do not believe me, at least believe my works, so that you may know that I am in the Father and the Father is in me." But when he was about to offer himself bodily for us, at the time when he went up to Jerusalem for this very purpose, he said to his disciples: "Sleep on now and take your rest; for look, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners." For his works led people to believe that he was true God, while his death showed that he truly had a body. So he rightly called the one being handed over "Son of Man"; for the Word is immortal and cannot be touched, and is Life itself. But the Pharisees did not believe even these things, nor were they willing to look at what their own sons were doing. So the Lord again gently refutes them, saying: "If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." Here too he said "by the Spirit of God" not because he is less than the Spirit, nor as though the Spirit were working these things in him. He said it to show once more that he himself, being the Word of God, works all things through the Spirit. He also wanted to teach his hearers that the more they attribute the works of the Spirit to Beelzebul, the more they slander the one who supplies the Spirit. For by saying this he also shows that they entangle themselves in such inescapable blasphemy not out of ignorance but willingly. And they are not ashamed. Although they know that such works belong to God, these senseless people attribute them to Beelzebul and said that these things came from an unclean spirit.

21. How then, when they dare such things, can they still find fault with the Greeks for fashioning idols and calling them gods? Their deeds are like the madness of those people, or perhaps their outrages are even greater, because they had received a law about this and yet dishonoured God by transgressing it. And what will these blasphemers do when they read the prophet Isaiah and hear that the signs of Christ's coming are sight for the blind, walking for the lame, speech for the mute, resurrection of the dead, healing of lepers, and the opening of the ears of the deaf? Whom will they want to be the doer of these things? If they say God, they will convict themselves of impiety against the Lord, for what the prophet foresaw and spoke, the Lord himself did when he was present. But if, carried away by rashness, they dare to say that these things too happen by Beelzebul, I fear that they will advance little by little in impiety. Then, when they read, "Who gave man a mouth? And who made the hard of hearing and the deaf, the seeing and the blind?" and similar passages, they will madly say that these words too belong to Beelzebul. For if they credit someone with the grace of giving sight, they must also make him the cause of not seeing, since the Word has said that the same one does both. And if they say this, they will surely come to think that Beelzebul is also the creator of human nature, for the one who makes something also has authority over what is made. Yet Moses said, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth," and, "In the image of God, God made man." And Daniel speaks boldly to Darius, saying: "I do not worship idols made with hands, but the living God, who created heaven and earth and has lordship over all flesh." Perhaps they will shift their ground again and say that blindness, lameness and the other afflictions come about as punishment from the Creator, while their removal and the kindness shown to the sufferers is the work of Beelzebul. But it is utterly silly even to consider this. Such foolish and impious talk belongs to madmen who have gone even further out of their minds, since these senseless people attribute even the better things, by comparison, not to God but to Beelzebul. They do not care whether they corrupt the teachings of the divine Scriptures, so long as they can deny the coming of Christ.

22. These wicked men should either not have despised the Lord as a man because of his bodily features, or else they should plainly have confessed him as true God because of his works as well. But they did everything perversely. Seeing a man, they reviled him as a man; beholding divine works, they denied his Godhead and ran to the devil, thinking that by daring such things they could escape being judged by the very Word whom they were insulting. Pharaoh's enchanters, magicians and sorcerers attempted a great deal, yet when they saw the signs done through Moses, they gave way and turned their backs, saying that the one doing these things was the finger of God. But the Pharisees and the scribes saw the whole hand of God at work [?], and beheld things greater than those signs being done through the Saviour himself. Yet they said that Beelzebul did them, the very one whom even the magicians, though he was their own, confessed could not do even lesser things than these. Who, then, can describe how far their madness goes? Or who, as the prophet said, will be able to compare anything to their impieties? For by comparison with themselves they have made even the people of Sodom look righteous. They have surpassed the ignorance of the Greeks and exceed the folly of Pharaoh's magicians. They can be compared only with the Ario-maniacs, since the two groups fall together into the same impiety. For the Jews, seeing the Father's works done through the Son, attribute them to Beelzebul. The Arians see the same works, yet they count the Lord who does them among the creatures, saying that he is from nothing and that "he was not before he was begotten." The Pharisees, seeing the Lord in the body, grumbled and said: "Why do you, being a man, make yourself God?" The Christ-fighters, seeing him suffer and sleep, blaspheme and say: "One who endures these things cannot be true God and of one substance with the Father." In short, if anyone wished to examine the evil minds of both side by side, he would find, as I said before, that together they fall into the salt valley of drunken folly. 23. For this reason the Lord declared that the punishment for such things would be unpardonable for both groups, saying: "Whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come." And rightly so. For if someone denies the Son, to whom can he appeal to gain forgiveness? Or what life or rest can a person expect if he has rejected the one who says, "I am the life," and, "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest"? Since these people pay such a penalty, it is clear what awaits those who are devout toward Christ. They worship both what in him is according to the flesh and what is according to the Spirit. They are not ignorant that he is the Son of God, nor do they deny that he also became Son of Man, but they believe that "In the beginning was the Word" and that "the Word became flesh." Such people will reign forever in the heavens, according to the holy promises of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ himself, who says: "Those will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life." I have written these things to you briefly, from what I have learned. Do not take them from me as a complete teaching, but only as a starting point. From now on, draw out the more exact meaning for yourself from the Gospel saying and from the Psalms, and bind up the sheaves of truth. Then, as you bring them in, those who sing the psalm may say: "They shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves." This we say in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom be glory and power to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
